主要内容: President-elect Donald Trump's proposed tariffs on Mexican cars may not stop the trend of U.S. automakers moving production to Mexico. Despite Trump's criticism of General Motors for building the Chevrolet Cruze in Mexico, Ford announced it would scrap plans to build a $1.6 billion plant there. U.S. automakers Ford, GM, and Fiat Chrysler are still planning to manufacture nearly 1 million more cars in Mexico by 2022, while producing half a million fewer in the U.S. Mexico's appeal lies in its trade agreements with 44 countries, giving automakers access to half the global car market tariff-free, compared to the U.S.'s 20 countries. Mexican workers are paid significantly less, with total hourly compensation in the motor vehicle manufacturing sector being about 80% less than in the U.S. This cost advantage, combined with trade agreements, makes Mexico an attractive location for automakers, even as Trump pushes for more protectionist policies. Automakers can save significant costs by producing vehicles in Mexico due to lower labor costs and favorable trade agreements. For a typical midsize car, an automaker can save $600 per vehicle on labor costs. However, additional shipping expenses to the U.S. and Europe add to the costs, making the overall savings from Mexico still substantial. Automakers save $1,500 per car on cheaper Mexican auto parts and that the U.S. lacks as many free trade agreements as Mexico, leading to higher costs for some parts if produced in the U.S. The cost advantages from Mexico’s trade agreements are significant, with automakers avoiding about $770 million in tariffs in 2014. Mexico sends 2 million cars a year to the U.S., more than half its total production, but by 2018, 28 percent of Mexico’s production will be exported to countries besides the U.S. and Canada. GM and Audi are examples of companies leveraging Mexico’s trade agreements to expand their markets.
